newsitem.title: USA: MGM to cut theme park size by nearly half.
newsitem.headline: MGM to cut theme park size by nearly half.

text.p: MGM Grand Inc, to accomodate a new $700 million expansion unveiled Tuesday, said it will cut the size of its struggling theme park to 18 acres from 33.

Shrinking the acreage of MGM Grand Adventures theme park will make room for a new spa and Marriott Marquis hotel, Alex Yemenidjian, president, said at the Oppenheimer Gaming and Lodging conference here.

Though it has consistenly lost money since opening in 1993, the theme park continues to generate "about $3.0 million in traffic" for the hotel and casino, making it an important entertainment venue for the resort to keep, he said.
Yemenidjian said MGM will remove unpopular rides but retain new ones like the "Sky Screamer" on the park's reduced grounds, and it will reconstruct the entrance.
"Having made about every mistake you can make in the theme park business over the last four years, we know what works and what doesn't," Yemenidjian said.

Earlier, MGM Grand unveiled a master plan to increase the size of the hotel's campus by spending $700 million to build the Marriott Marquis, an upscale Ritz Carlton hotel, several other amenities and an exclusive "Mansion" for high-rollers.

"To stay at the 'Mansion' you have to have a major credit line," Yemenidjian said, adding a smile. "It doesn't matter whether you are Bill Clinton or Bill Gates, you have to have a major credit line."

Though the expansion aims to add to MGM Grand's current strong base of high-rolling gamblers, a major benefit comes from bringing MGM Grand into Marriott's massive reservation system a full two years before the Marriott Marquis is built.
Currently, Marriott International Inc receives about 10 million calls a year requesting rooms in Las Vegas, but Marriott does not have a hotel in Las Vegas.
Those calls will be funneled to MGM Grand soon after a definitive agreement is signed by the companies. The Marriott Marquis, however, will not open until at least 1999.

Yemenidjian said a quick analysis of the impact of Marriott's reservation system shows $24.6 million could be added to MGM's bottom line over two years, before taxes. The company calculated that number by estimating the reservation system could fill 80 percent of MGM Grand's currently unoccupied rooms on an average week, from Sunday through Thursday.
